title: Fables of the Gods
english: …Having asked for the desirable thing, as he himself says, he composed fables. He collected fables. He writes of the birth of a song, guiding us on a journey of stories, mentioning Earth and Coeus and Hyperion, and in addition to these, Iapetus and Prometheus, who stole fire from Jupiter, and a woman, and how the human race would have been established, or how the gods, some of whom are immortal, would have been the creators of mortal things, as Plato thought. These ideas are opposed to the writings of the all-wise Moses. Yet the Mosaic writings were opposed by the poets' art, which permits them to mythologize without restraint, although perhaps they should not. For perhaps the law of the poets is to mythologize without restraint. If they say nothing necessary, let their stories not be believed; and if they say anything about the gods, let their fables and nonsense be disbelieved. Rather, the true and proven words should be accepted; and the historians like Herodotus and the poets like Hesiod and Homer are to be considered. These are the ones who, having composed history in this way, handed down the origin of the gods, gave them honors and arts, and formed their appearance. They are the ones who, having given the gods names, honors, and appearance, wrote myths about them, and those who honored them, and those who seem to be later, and those who gave them names, honors, and appearance, and those who wrote about their deeds. If they only wrote fables and nothing else, they should be ridiculed by right; but if they truly honored them, they should be respected. For why do they call upon Therus and consider those named by them as worthy, when they write about gods in vain, as if they have been deceived, and they accept some of their statements but not others, if indeed they say anything worthy, or how the gods might have become creators in some other way? They do not repudiate the theogony of Hesiod, from which they boast, yet they do not believe in the other things they say, and they do not think it is any of their business to investigate these matters. They do not think Plato is worthy, and they do not think the gods are worthy, and they do not think they can be hidden or forced. For they say that if the gods do not exist, then nothing can be hidden or forced, and they say that the gods are not able to be killed or forced. Instead, they say that we should not investigate these things, but rather the things that are said by the poets, who have written about the origins of the gods. The pagans believe that the gods can be appeased by sacrifices, prayers, and gifts, and they confess that they have been deceived. Let everything that is said by them be disbelieved (Isaiah 29:13). When poets have given genealogies, but they themselves are, indeed, to be known, and the shameful things about them, which they have become like sacrifices, they have spoken about the earth and the sea, and the offspring of the gods, and the brothers of the gods, and the shameful things of the doctrines, and the fictions of the poets, and the names of the gods, and the things that are said about them. Hesiod has said things about the gods that are not to be despised, and they have spoken about the earth and the sea, and the offspring of the gods, and the brothers of the gods, and the shameful things of the doctrines, and the fictions of the poets, and the names of the gods, and the things that are said about them. Leaving the woman and the word about her, we will accept Hesiod's Pandora rather, for it seems to be the optimum thing to do. In her, the things from God are said; she was made as if formed by God for the assistance of a man; but nothing of this sort is provided, on the contrary, it is seen as contemptible …
